documents.t: Hiring a team to build software usually means trusting a process you can't see. These pages show every step of how we work, and list what moves into your name at the end, so you know both before you send a word. Zaions is a software agency. We build web and Android apps, browser extensions and desktop apps, and we do the design, video, QA and AI work around them. We also built and still run 15+ products of our own. Four steps, every project. You send the brief. You get a written plan and estimate before we write a line of code. Every milestone ends with a link to the working build, so you click through progress instead of reading a status report, and at handover the code, the design files, the accounts and every credential move into your name. documents.t: You, if you're thinking about hiring us, or you already have. They're written for founders and small-business owners who know what the business needs and don't want to babysit developers to get it. We assume no technical background. Where a technical word is unavoidable, it comes with its meaning in the same sentence, like a code repository, where all your source code lives.

zaions.com is the short version. These pages are the long one. The agency site tells you what we do and shows the products we run. The docs explain how each part of a project works: what a good brief contains, what a milestone link opens, what moves into your name at handover, and how to pay an invoice once you're a client. These pages quote a few figures, like the package prices and the phone number. zaions.com is the authority for them, and where the two differ, zaions.com wins: the current package prices, on Pricing (opens in a new tab) the payment methods, which only zaions.com lists, on Payments (opens in a new tab) the phone number and email addresses, on Contact (opens in a new tab) If a figure here differs from your written estimate, the figures in your estimate are the ones for your project. These pages are written for everyone.

documents.t: A good brief says what the product must do, who will use it, and roughly what you can spend. That's enough for us to reply with questions or a time for the free call. Only your name and email are required. The brief is the form at zaions.com/start-a-project (opens in a new tab). It has three short steps.

Three things matter most. Everything else helps. What it must do. The jobs a person gets done with it, in your words. "Customers book a table and get a reminder" beats "a booking platform". Who will use it. Your customers, your staff, or both. On a phone, a computer, or each. Your budget range. A rough range is enough. It helps us shape the estimate. If your idea is still a napkin sketch, that's a fine place to start. Send it as it is.

Skip any field you're unsure of. It can wait for the free call or the written plan. Step Field What to put there 1 · Your project Services Pick any that fit: web apps, mobile apps, browser extensions, desktop apps, graphic design, video editing, QA testing and automation, AI features and automation. Not sure? Skip it. 1 · Your project What you need What it must do and who will use it. You can bold a line or make a bulleted list of features. Links to examples go here too. 2 · Budget and timing Package The package closest to your budget; Packages explained covers each one. Arriving from a package's button picks it for you; change it any time. 2 · Budget and timing Budget range One of five bands, from under $1,000 to $5,000 or more, or "Not sure yet". No band is too small to send. The bands follow the package floors on Pricing (opens in a new tab). 2 · Budget and timing Your target date A launch, event or deadline you're working toward. It's your date, and it helps the plan. 3 · About you Your name, Email, Company We reply to the email you type, so check it once. Company is optional. There's no upload field. Put links to sketches, documents, a shared folder or a competitor you like inside "What you need", and they reach us along with the brief.

Example, not a client. An illustration of the shape, written for these docs. Services: Web apps, Mobile apps What you need: I run a small bakery. Customers should be able to order a cake online, pick a pickup day and pay a deposit, and my two staff need one screen showing tomorrow's orders before they open. Most customers order from their phones, and most of them use Android. Package: Build · Budget range: $3,000 to $5,000 · Target date: a date before the holiday season Why it works: it names the people (customers and two staff), the jobs (order, pick a day, pay a deposit, see tomorrow's orders) and the device. It doesn't name a framework, a database or a feature list copied from someone else's app. That part's our job. The written plan shows you what we chose and why.

Every handover covers these five, wherever they apply to your project: The code repository, where all your source code lives The design files, editable, so the next designer starts from ours The store accounts: Google Play, the Chrome Web Store, or whichever your product ships to The hosting accounts, along with the domain settings Every credential and password the product needs to run Nothing stays on our side that you'd need to keep running it, change it or hand it to another team.

For hosting and services, yours if you like. Otherwise, test accounts. You can bring your own hosting and service accounts from the start, so they sit in your name from the first milestone. If you'd rather not, we set up test accounts for your project and share them with you from day one, logins included. You can replace any of them with your own at any point. Either way, there's no password exchange to arrange at the end: test-account logins are yours from day one, and your own accounts were yours all along.

documents.t: Three of our tools are open source, one per operating system: windowsweep for Windows, macleanup for macOS and linux-cleanup for Linux. Each reclaims disk space a developer's machine loses to caches and build leftovers, and each is MIT-licensed in a public repository you can read line by line. Both windowsweep and macleanup name every path before touching it. On Linux, linux-cleanup asks before each category, and --scan prints every target first. Client work stays private unless the client asks us to show it. These three are our own. Start a project (opens in a new tab)Book a free consultation (opens in a new tab)

To clear the places a system cleaner doesn't know about: package caches, build caches, emulator images, node_modules for a project you finished months ago. Clearing them by hand means keeping your own list of paths and remembering which ones are safe. These tools carry that list, and they're careful by design: each one deletes files, and each README says plainly which deletions can't be undone.

A developer-aware cleanup tool for Windows 10 (1809 and later) and Windows 11. It runs with nothing to install through npx windowsweep, refuses personal folders outright, never follows a junction (a folder shortcut that points elsewhere on the disk), and by default keeps any cache you've used in the last 100 days. Start with npx windowsweep --scan, which deletes nothing. The command-line tool makes no network calls at all. It also ships as a Windows desktop app: a window that drives the same engine, released as .exe and .msi installers. Two limits. The installer isn't signed with a paid code-signing certificate, so Windows SmartScreen warns the first time it runs; every release carries a signature the app's own updater checks, plus a SHA-256 checksum, a fingerprint of the file that shows it hasn't changed. And unlike the command line, the window sends usage and crash reports, with no switch to turn them off; its README lists what's never sent, including file paths, folder names and your user name. Repository and README (opens in a new tab) · Releases (opens in a new tab)

A cleanup tool for macOS 11 Big Sur or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel, covering 28 sections from developer caches to unused apps. Every destructive section asks first by default, and --dry-run never touches the disk. The whole tool is two readable files you can inspect before running it. No telemetry, and no network call unless you ask it to check for an update. Some sections delete permanently, emptying the Trash among them, and the README marks each one. Repository and README (opens in a new tab)

A Bash cleanup tool for Linux, including WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux, which runs Linux inside Windows). You run it with npx linux-cleanup. By default it deletes only files untouched for 100+ days, refuses to work inside your personal directories, and makes no network calls of any kind. Deletion is permanent. There's no undo, so start with npx linux-cleanup --scan, which prints what it would reclaim and deletes nothing. Repository and README (opens in a new tab)

The same habits run through client work. The windowsweep repository runs its checks on every change, and you can open the check history (opens in a new tab) to see what ran and whether it passed. Its Windows app is live. It's our one desktop app today. If you need a desktop app or a command-line tool of your own, it goes through the same four steps as any project, and its brief gets its own written estimate. Desktop apps install on Windows, Linux or macOS, and the estimate names how signing is arranged for your project, along with any code-signing certificate or store fee your installers need.

They're listed in your estimate, separate from the price. That list runs from the domain and an email service to the Google Play registration for an Android app, plus hosting and any third-party service your product uses. We design for free tiers where your product allows. They continue after handover. They're billed to your own accounts.

On zaions.com, not here. We keep the methods and their account details in one place, the Payments (opens in a new tab) page, so a detail is never out of date on a second copy. Each method is a card with its details listed, and every detail has a Copy button beside it. Copying keeps each detail exactly as it's written. The button says "Copied" once it has worked, and a screen reader hears which detail it copied. Old links still work. An address ending in /pay, /payment or /payment-details opens the same page.

Your written estimate sets the schedule. You agree to it before any work starts, so there's no payment you haven't already seen in writing. Team is paid monthly. The package runs to the end of the month you paid for, and the maintenance add-on is monthly too, priced in your estimate. A change in scope never adds a payment you haven't agreed to.
